source.title: Defenses at Odds: Measuring and Explaining Defense Conflicts in Large Language Models
source.authors: Xiang Meng; Wen-Yu Chen; Chuan-Chao Zang; Xin-Yu Gao; Jia-Ning Wang; Li Wang; Zheng Li; Shan-Qing Guo

record.tranche_reason: Extends evidence about later model updates weakening safety to sequential applications of other defenses. It measures harmful-prompt safety risk after those updates, but does not test the specific data regimes or first-token claims in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates safety risk (ASR) as one part of sequential defense compatibility. Its later updates are privacy or fairness defenses, not fine-tuning on a few harmful examples or ordinary benign instruction data. It does not measure per-token KL, opening-token bypasses, or localized safety weights. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Safety-first compositions apply a non-harmful later update (TOFU unlearning via NPO/RMU, StereoSet debiasing via Unbias/TV) to a safety-defended instruct model. They then measure harmful-prompt ASR on 404 SALAD-Bench prompts before and after. This bears on V2 (non-harmful later training raising harmful compliance) in a new setting. The later updates are unlearning/editing objectives rather than ordinary instruction fine-tuning, so it is T3, not T1/T2. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude that later defenses can preserve, strengthen or weaken earlier protection depending on pair, order and model. They present representational counteraction as one possible pathway, and CTDR reduced regression in six selected conflicts while keeping roughly 97% or more of G2.
record.recipe_differences: Studies sequential compositions of independently configured safety, privacy, and fairness defenses, rather than fine-tuning safety-trained models on the harmful or benign example sets in the cited works. It does not test first-token concentration or bypass methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Safety-risk outcomes vary across model, defense pair, and application order. The authors report a single training realization per composition; behavioral ASR averages over three decoding seeds.

fits_no_version.finding: In 11 selected cases, negative pooled RDC along the first-risk direction accompanied all eight regressions. CTDR penalizing opposing shifts cut safety RRR to ≤0 in four safety-first conflicts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Later training erodes safety by counteracting earlier safety-supporting activation shifts, and penalizing this counteraction preserves safety.

record.problems: Each configured composition has a single training realization, so the conflict counts do not estimate seed-level prevalence. Representational analysis covers 11 selected cases and CTDR is evaluated on six selected conflicts. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the safety-risk composition results, although ASR is averaged over three decoding seeds.
record.rows_left_out: No safety-first ASR compositions were omitted. Other risk-dimension outcomes and the MMLU utility table were not included because they do not measure the claim's harmful-response safety behavior. Rows R54–R57 are representational measurements, not behavioral compliance rates.

untested.parts: No ordinary instruction-data or carefully selected benign fine-tuning. Later updates are unlearning/debiasing objectives.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No prefill, suffix or decoding-change attacks.
Layer support sets are found by activation patching, but there is no test that a small set of weights carries safety.
No test of why safety is shallow.
CTDR is a directional-retention penalty, not token-depth deepening. Its durability against fine-tuning attacks is not tested.

missing.what: Safety ASR after a privacy/fairness defense applied directly to M0, versus M0 ASR. Example: Llama-S M0 0.6535 vs 0.5421 after NPO, 0.5528 after Unbias, 0.5710 after TV. These benign-update effects are not recorded as rows.
missing.locator: Table 6 vs Tables 7–9, Subsequent M1 column for DPO(S)/CAT(S) rows

record.verdict_notes: Linking to V2 is a judgement call. The later updates are not harmful, but they are unlearning (NPO/RMU on TOFU) or debiasing (Unbias, TV editing), not ordinary benign instruction tuning. The paper itself frames the work as extending Qi et al. on benign fine-tuning. M0 is each instruct model already fine-tuned on TOFU, and no pre-TOFU ASR is reported. Eval prompts were selected to elicit harm from at least one M0. Each composition is a single training run, and no uncertainty is reported for the ASR differences, so small changes are treated as absent. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples; no test of harmful-example fine-tuning removing refusal.
No ordinary or carefully chosen benign instruction-data fine-tuning.
No per-token KL measurement between aligned and base models.
No compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding-change bypass tests.
No test of whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
No test of why safety behavior is shallow or of whether data or an objective produces first-token concentration.
CTDR aims to retain earlier-defense changes during a different subsequent defense; it does not train safety beyond the first tokens or test whether such deepening holds up.

relationships.condition: Selected safety-first compositions, chiefly DPO followed by NPO/Unbias/TV on Gemma-S and TV/Unbias after CAT on Gemma-L and Qwen
relationships.reason: Harmful-prompt ASR rose after non-harmful later updates: Gemma-S RRR 0.697/0.798/0.505 (R17, R19, R20). Qwen-L CAT→TV rose 0.006→0.287 (R48). Smaller rises appear in R01, R02, R29, R31, R40.
relationships.display_finding: Harmful-prompt attack success rose after the later non-harmful updates, with RRR of 0.697, 0.798 and 0.505 on Gemma-S and a rise from 0.006 to 0.287 for Qwen-L CAT followed by TV; smaller rises appeared in other compositions.

relationships.condition: Across all 48 safety-first compositions and six models
relationships.reason: Erosion occurred in only 18 of 48 compositions and depended on model, defense pair and order (R49). Many rises were small (R16, R18, R21, R27, R30, R37, R39), and several changes were negligible (R14, R26, R41, R45–R47).
relationships.display_finding: Erosion appeared in only 18 of 48 compositions and depended on model, defense pair and order; many rises were small and several changes negligible.

relationships.condition: Llama-L and Qwen DPO-first compositions, most CAT-first compositions on Llama-S, and TV after DPO on all models
relationships.reason: Later privacy/fairness updates lowered harmful ASR. Examples: Llama-L DPO→TV 0.529→0.199 (R12), Qwen-L DPO→TV 0.553→0.187 (R44), Gemma-L DPO→NPO 0.267→0.144 (R25).
relationships.display_finding: Later privacy or fairness updates lowered harmful attack success, for example Llama-L DPO then TV from 0.529 to 0.199, Qwen-L DPO then TV from 0.553 to 0.187, and Gemma-L DPO then NPO from 0.267 to 0.144.
